unitDescription.value: In this unit, students investigate the relationship between hardware specifications and system performance using mBot robots. They apply systems thinking to explain how specific hardware components and sensor capabilities affect a robot's functionality, selecting appropriate hardware for particular tasks and workloads. Students apply computational thinking to decompose real-world problems, representing algorithmic solutions through flowcharts and pseudocode before implementing them in a programming environment. This involves the use of control structures, including selection and repetition, to process sensor input and automate physical movement. Through divergent design thinking techniques, students generate and review ideas against established design criteria and user stories to ensure solutions meet specific needs. The unit is framed around a search-and-rescue mission, requiring students to iteratively test and debug their robotic solutions to ensure they meet safety and performance specifications.

cohortAndClassConsiderations.value: In Digital Technologies, students should have frequent opportunities for authentic learning by making key connections with other learning areas.

description.value: Students design and develop an autonomous robotic solution using the MBot platform to navigate a complex course. They apply systems thinking to explain how hardware specifications and sensor capabilities affect performance, justifying their selection of specific components for the required navigation tasks. Using computational thinking, students decompose the problem into logical components and represent their solutions through flowcharts and pseudocode before implementation in a general-purpose programming language. The project requires students to iteratively test and debug their algorithms, evaluating the final prototype against design criteria and user stories to ensure the hardware effectively supports the intended performance workloads and functional requirements.

conditions.value: 3–5 A3 pages or equivalent digital media pages; includes annotated graphical representations, algorithm designs (flowcharts/pseudocode), and a video demonstration of the physical prototype (maximum 2 minutes).

achievementStandard.value: By the end of Year 8, students explain how digital systems represent data as binary and how data is transmitted in networks. They explain the need for personal security controls to protect data and investigate how hardware components and specifications affect the performance of digital systems. Students apply computational thinking to define and decompose real-world problems. They design user experiences and represent algorithmic solutions using flowcharts and pseudocode. Students implement these solutions in general-purpose programming environments, using control structures including selection and repetition to process sensor inputs and automate responses. They iteratively test and debug their programs to ensure they meet specifications. Students evaluate existing and student-created solutions against design criteria and user stories. They acquire, validate and model data from sensors and other sources, analysing and visualising it to extract meaning. Students plan and manage projects individually and collaboratively, using digital tools to create and communicate content responsibly.

activities.title: Deconstructing Movement Bugs and Parameter Holes
activities.teacherDoes: Present an intentional buggy drive script on the screen where an mBot overshoots a 50cm target by 25cm due to an uncalibrated wait parameter. Model the systematic debugging protocol: 1. Measure physical error, 2. Isolate corresponding code parameter, 3. Calculate corrected parameter value, 4. Re-test. Emphasise how physical constraints like wheel slippage and battery voltage require empirical calibration rather than guesswork.
activities.studentsDo: Analyze the buggy code snippet displayed and in your workbook. Identify the logical parameter causing the distance overshoot and fill in the missing duration value to correct the 45cm movement.

activities.questioning:
Why can we not rely purely on mathematical distance calculations when programming physical robots? Expected: Physical factors such as surface friction, tyre traction, and battery charge levels alter actual speed and stopping distance.
What algorithmic error occurs if the delay command is placed before the motor drive block? Expected: The program pauses before activating the motors, delaying execution without controlling drive duration.
activities.scaffolding: Reference calculation: At motor power 100, mBot travels approximately 30cm per second. Target distance: 45cm. Calculated delay: 45 / 30 = 1.5 seconds.
activities.eLearning: Display code snippet on projector; students keep laptops closed during explicit modelling.

activities.teacherDoes: Guide student pairs through testing a two-segment path (drive forward 80cm, turn right 90 degrees). activities.questioning:
If your mBot rotates 110 degrees instead of 90 degrees, which specific parameter should be adjusted? Expected: Reduce the duration of the turn delay block or lower the turn motor power setting.
How does battery discharge over multiple test runs impact distance precision? Expected: As battery voltage sags, motor RPM decreases, causing fixed-duration drive commands to cover progressively shorter distances.

Expected: It must emit the high-frequency sonic burst and subsequently capture the returning echo to determine elapsed time.

Expected: Sound energy disperses and weakens over distance in air, meaning reflections from very distant objects are too faint for the transducer to register.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for reference:
- Ultrasonic Sensor: An electronic peripheral that measures distance by transmitting and receiving ultrasonic sound waves.
- Transducer: A hardware component that converts electrical signals into acoustic vibrations and vice versa.
- Time of Flight: The total round-trip time taken by an acoustic wave to travel from the transmitter to an obstacle and return to the receiver.
- Echo: The reflected acoustic sound wave detected after colliding with a physical surface.

activities.title: Reactive Robotics Vocabulary and Sensor Mechanics

Why is the elapsed time divided by two in the Time of Flight distance calculation? Expected: Sound must travel to the obstacle and reflect back, meaning total transit time represents double the one-way distance.
Why does an autonomous system require continuous sensor polling rather than a single check at startup? Expected: Dynamic environments change continuously, so the robot must constantly poll inputs to make timely reactive decisions before collisions occur.
activities.scaffolding: Defined terms provided on board and workbook: Ultrasonic Sensor (hardware emitting/receiving high-frequency sound to calculate distance), Time of Flight (transit time of emitted sound wave reflecting off an object), Sense-Think-Act Cycle (continuous loop: sample sensors, evaluate selection logic, execute motor output), Threshold (numerical boundary value that triggers a conditional state change).

lessons.title: Proportional Control and Advanced Line-Following
lessons.learningGoal: Implement proportional control logic to improve mBot line-following smoothness

orientate.smartStart: Students complete a checklist in their workbook assessing the hardware components required for precision line-tracking.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can apply proportional control logic to calibrate mBot line-following behaviour

activities.title: Proportional Control Concepts
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly model how binary on-off logic causes oscillatory, jerky robot movement by abruptly switching motor power between maximum and zero. Contrast this with proportional control, which scales motor speed adjustments continuously based on the magnitude of the sensor error value. Demonstrate the calculation of an error variable ($e = 	ext{leftSensor} - 	ext{rightSensor}$) and explain how multiplying this error by a tuning constant ($K_p$) dynamically corrects steering.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher demonstration, analyse the operational differences between binary and proportional feedback loops, and complete the classification audit in the workbook table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Examine the feature characteristics in the workbook table and tick the correct boxes to classify binary control versus proportional control.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why is binary on-off line-following inherently inefficient on complex, winding tracks?
Expected: It causes the robot to oscillate wildly from side to side because motors only operate at fixed maximum or zero power without grading the response.
prompt: How does scaling the motor speed adjustment by an error magnitude improve navigation smoothness?
Expected: Minor deviations receive small corrections while large deviations receive strong corrections, preventing overshooting and maintaining momentum.
activities.scaffolding: Binary control uses discrete on-off states (e.g., motor full on or full off) resulting in constant course correction oscillation. Proportional control (P-control) uses continuous mathematical feedback where the correction output is directly proportional to the size of the error signal: $\text{Correction} = K_p \times \text{Error}$.
activities.eLearning: Laptops down during direct instruction and teacher-led whiteboard modeling.
activities.transition: Transition directly into co-constructing the mBlock proportional logic script in the subsequent guided activity.

workbookSpec.title: Control System Classification Audit
workbookSpec.prompt: Tick the correct operational characteristics for each control logic type.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Binary Control: Jerky movement, Fixed power output. Proportional Control: Smooth trajectory, Scaled power output.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Movement Trajectory -> Binary Control: Jerky; Proportional Control: Smooth. Motor Power Scaling -> Binary Control: Fixed power; Proportional Control: Scaled by error.

activities.title: Co-Constructing Proportional Logic
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through co-constructing an mBlock script on the board that uses mathematical operators and variables to calculate motor speed corrections based on sensor intensity. Model how the error value dynamically adjusts left and right motor outputs. Script: 'Notice how subtracting the target threshold from the current light sensor reading gives us our error value. If the error is zero, the mBot drives straight at base speed.'
activities.studentsDo: Follow along on their devices to build the proportional control script in mBlock 5 and complete the missing holes in their workbook code analysis task.
activities.visibleInstructions: Examine the provided mBlock script snippet and fill in the missing variable name used to store the calculated sensor error.
activities.questioning:
prompt: What mathematical operation is typically used to calculate the steering correction offset?
expected: Subtraction of the current sensor reading from the target threshold to find the error.
prompt: Why do we add and subtract the error value from the base motor speed?
expected: To proportionally increase one motor's speed while decreasing the other's, steering the mBot back toward the line.
activities.scaffolding: Code structure reference: set [error v] to (sensor value) - (target threshold). set motor left speed to (base speed + {{1}}). set motor right speed to (base speed - {{1}}).
activities.eLearning: Students open mBlock 5 on their laptops and follow the co-constructed script development.
activities.transition: Transition to independent coding and testing of the proportional algorithm on the physical tracks.

activities.title: Testing and Calibrating Line-Followers
activities.teacherDoes: Supervise student testing on physical tracks, checking that groups are adjusting their threshold values effectively. Model how to isolate variables during testing: 'Notice how Trial 2 increased the base speed while raising the scaling factor. If the mBot oscillates too wildly, reduce the scaling factor before lowering the base speed.'
activities.studentsDo: Upload the script to their mBot, execute test runs on the physical line-following track, and record performance data and observations in their workbook table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Conduct the three test trials on the track, recording stability outcomes and adjusting scaling factors to optimise your mBot's cornering performance.
activities.questioning:
prompt: How did adjusting the scaling factor change your mBot's cornering ability?
Expected: Increasing the scaling factor made steering sharper and more responsive, but excessive values caused severe oscillation or loss of the line.
prompt: Why is it necessary to record multiple trials instead of relying on a single test?
Expected: Empirical testing across varying speeds accounts for external variables like battery voltage drop and ambient lighting changes.
activities.scaffolding:
Test table structure:
- Trial 1: Base Speed 40, Scaling Factor 1.0 (Baseline)
- Trial 2: Base Speed 60, Scaling Factor 1.5 (Moderate adjustment)
- Trial 3: Base Speed 60, Scaling Factor 2.0 (Aggressive correction)
Result options to record: Stable / Oscillation / Lost Line.
activities.eLearning: Active monitoring of student groups working with mBots and physical tracking surfaces.
activities.transition: Pack down testing equipment and transition to the Culminate stage to summarise findings.

workbookSpec.title: Proportional Control Calibration Log
workbookSpec.prompt: Record the stability outcome for each experimental trial testing different base speeds and error scaling factors.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Trial 1: Stable (smooth tracking at low speed). Trial 2: Stable with minor oscillation on sharp turns. Trial 3: Lost Line (scaling factor too aggressive for surface friction).

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Results will vary based on track surface friction and ambient lighting; students should conclude that higher scaling factors paired with high base speeds lead to tracking loss and system instability.

lessons.title: Line-Lost Recovery Logic and Final Rescue Challenge Trials
lessons.learningGoal: Design and implement corrective recovery logic to handle line-lost scenarios during autonomous navigation

orientate.smartStart: Students rank a scrambled list of recovery behaviours in their workbook from most efficient to least efficient.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can program an mBot to autonomously recover its path when it loses the line

activities.title: Deconstructing Line-Lost Scenarios
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate how a rescue robot handles unexpected gaps or acute angles where line-tracking sensors lose the path. Model the systematic breakdown of conditional fallback logic using closed-loop system principles. Explain how continuous sensor feedback determines whether the mBot executes a sweeping search or maintains directional momentum.
activities.studentsDo: Examine the recovery flow diagram on the board and complete the matching task in your workbook to align sensor states with appropriate corrective actions.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each recovery action from the bank to the corresponding sensor state condition in the workbook table.
activities.questioning:
prompt: What specific robotic behaviour should execute if both line-tracking sensors detect white flooring simultaneously?
expected: Execute a sweeping pivot search to re-locate the line based on the last known heading.
prompt: Why is proportional feedback insufficient when an mBot completely loses the tracking line?
expected: Proportional control requires a valid error signal from the sensors; zero signal means the mathematical error cannot be calculated, necessitating discrete fallback logic.
activities.scaffolding: Reference definitions: Both sensors white -> pivot left/right to sweep. Left sensor black -> steer left to centre. Right sensor black -> steer right to centre. Closed-loop systems rely on continuous sensor output directly influencing motor input to maintain the desired trajectory.
activities.eLearning: Follow along with the digital flowchart projected on the main display before accessing local mBlock environments.
activities.transition: Transition into co-constructing the line-lost recovery algorithm within mBlock 5.

workbookSpec.title: Line-Lost Recovery Action Matching
workbookSpec.prompt: Match each sensor state condition to its correct autonomous recovery action.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1. Both sensors off line -> Pivot search to sweep and find path. 2. Left sensor on line -> Steer left to correct trajectory. 3. Right sensor on line -> Steer right to correct trajectory.
bank: Pivot search to sweep and find path
Steer left to correct trajectory
Steer right to correct trajectory

activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1. Both sensors off line -> Pivot search to sweep and find path. 2. Left sensor on line -> Steer left to correct trajectory. 3. Right sensor on line -> Steer right to correct trajectory.

activities.title: Building Recovery Control Structures
activities.teacherDoes: Model the logical sequence for line-lost recovery on the board, demonstrating how nested conditional statements operate within a continuous loop. Explain: "When both line-tracking sensors read white, the robot has lost the path and must initiate a systematic sweep." Guide students through mapping this subroutine into their workbook flow diagrams before writing the mBlock code.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the missing stages in the flow diagram workbook activity, detailing the decision branch and recovery sweep actions.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the missing control block stages in your workbook flow diagram to map the line-lost recovery algorithm.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why must the recovery loop include a time-out condition or rotation limit?
Expected: So the robot does not spin indefinitely searching for a line if it has been removed from the track entirely.
prompt: How does the conditional branch determine whether to turn left or right during recovery?
Expected: By checking which sensor last detected the black line, indicating the probable direction of the track.
activities.scaffolding:
Recovery Algorithm Logic:
1. Check Left and Right line sensors.
2. Decision: Are both sensors reading white (off the line)?
- Yes: Execute sweep subroutine (turn right at low speed until a sensor detects black).
- No: Continue standard proportional line-following routine.
activities.eLearning: Students use mBlock 5 to program and test the nested conditional statements on their hardware.
activities.transition: Transition directly to the final practical rescue challenge trials on the test course.

workbookSpec.title: Line-Lost Recovery Flowchart
workbookSpec.prompt: Complete the flowchart stages to map the robot's automated recovery sequence when sensors lose the line.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Check Sensors -> Both White? -> Yes -> Turn Right (Sweep) -> Sensor Detects Black -> Resume Tracking -> End

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Stages must accurately reflect: 1. Read Line Sensors -> 2. Evaluate condition (Both White?) -> 3. Branch Yes: Execute search sweep / Branch No: Continue normal tracking -> 4. Re-engage main loop once line is re-detected.

activities.title: Final Rescue Challenge Trials
activities.teacherDoes: Oversee final rescue challenge trials, ensuring safety protocols and recording video evidence of autonomous recovery runs. Model rigorous testing procedures by demonstrating how to systematically verify each operational requirement on the evaluation checklist before declaring a trial successful.
activities.studentsDo: Run their final autonomous navigation test on the complex course, recording performance outcomes and verifying each functional criterion in their workbook checklist.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the final evaluation checklist in your workbook confirming successful course navigation and line-loss recovery performance.
activities.questioning:
q: How effectively did your recovery logic handle the sharp turns and line-loss scenarios on the test course?
Expected: Student responses should reference whether the sweep search successfully re-acquired the line without manual intervention and how smoothly the robot transitioned back to normal tracking.
q: What adjustments were necessary during trials to accommodate hardware response times or surface variations?
Expected: Students should explain sensor threshold calibrations and speed modifications made to prevent overshoot during high-speed sections.
activities.scaffolding: Checklist criteria for successful rescue mission: 1. Stable line-tracking, 2. Reliable line-loss detection, 3. Autonomous recovery sweep execution, 4. Full course completion without manual intervention.
activities.eLearning: Teacher monitors student robot runs and records final performance evidence for unit assessment.
